title: Sola fide: not legal perfection, free pardon; Rome can admit this sense
source_text: LV. Praeterea in quaestione est, an fides sola justificet, an vero etiam opera. Et quidem fidem solam justificare, non opera, pretendunt Doctores Scholae Reformatae, sicuti jam observavimus. Sed in eo mens eorum est, ad hoc ut justi habeamur, & absolvamur in Dei judicio, non exigi a nobis opera, quae lex, gratiae opposita, postulat ad peccatoris justificationem, id est, omnibus numeris absolutam legis observationem, quae omne peccatum, & omnem omnino transgressionem excludit, sed sufficere ut credamus in Christum fide viva, & per bona opera efficaci: etiamsi ante peccato servierimus, & postea non desinamus multis, ex infirmitate, lapsibus esse obnoxii. Ac praeterea, quum opera justificare negant, per id significare volunt, condonationem peccatorum nostrorum, & absolutionem ab illorum reatu in Dei judicio, gratuitam esse, & nullis operum meritis deberi: tum etiam nullas virtutes, nec ulla nostra constituere justitiam talem, quae possit districto Dei judicio opponi, & per quam, si Deus nos severe examinet, nec ullam nobis gratiam faciat, mortem aeternam evadere, & ad beatam immortalitatem pervenire queamus: quae omnia facile admittit Schola Romana.
pass_a_gloss: Further it is in question whether faith alone justifies, or works also. And indeed the Doctors of the Reformed School contend that faith alone justifies, not works, as we have already observed. But in this their mind is that in order that we be held just and be absolved in God's judgment, there are not required of us the works which the law opposed to grace demands for a sinner's justification—that is, observation of the law complete in every respect, which excludes every sin and every transgression whatsoever—but that it suffices that we believe in Christ with living faith efficacious through good works: even if beforehand we served sin, and afterward do not cease from weakness to be liable to many falls. And further, when they deny that works justify, by that they mean to signify that the condoning of our sins and absolution from their guilt in God's judgment is gratuitous and owed to no merits of works; and also that no virtues, nor anything of ours, constitute such a righteousness as can be opposed to God's strict judgment, and by which, if God should examine us severely and grant us no grace, we could escape eternal death and arrive at blessed immortality: all which the Roman School easily admits.
pass_b_english: Reformed sola fide: not legal-covenant perfection, but living faith; pardon free, no inherent justice that stands strict judgment.
Rome can easily admit this sense of the exclusion of works.
